name: Odoodee
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Tone. There is a two-way tone contrast at word level. A high ‘accent’ is realised by a level pitch on the word. A low ‘accent’ is realised by a falling pitch on the last syllable of the word. In the orthography, high pitch is signalled with an acute accent mark on the last vowel of the word. [...] E.g. só ‘bird’ / so ‘dog’; í ‘tongue’ / i ‘storm’. Length. Length is not contrastive. Vowel length is conditioned by stress, i.e. stressed syllables have longer vowels. Stress. Stress does not seem to be predictable. More testing needs to be done. Stress was found to be contrastive on only one word ( /ˈkɔlɔ/ ‘bamboo’ vs. /kɔˈlɔ/ ‘skin’ ). Stress is not marked on this word.
new_statements.citation: Hays, Darrell & Kerttu Hays. 2004. Organised Phonology Data: Odoodee (Kalamo) Language [KKC], Western Province. Ukarumpa: SIL-PNG unpublished ms., 7 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives 42256).
new_statements.locator: p. 4, section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)', subsections Tone / Length / Stress
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (7 pp., pdfinfo Title 'OPD', Author 'Darrell Lee Hays', created 2004-08-31; header 'Odoodee (Kalamo) OPD Printed: September 1, 2004'). Page 4, heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' with subsections Tone / Length / Stress: the quoted passage is there word for word (text layer, lines 145-157 of; the '[...]' in the report elides only 'High pitch is only marked on words that contrast with a word having low pitch. Low pitch is not marked.'). The text layer drops the IPA, so I rendered p.4 at 150 dpi and read it as an image: the minimal pair is printed / ˈkɔlɔ / 'bamboo' vs. / kɔˈlɔ / 'skin', exactly as reported, and the Syllable Patterns table bolds one syllable per word…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Odoodee has a two-way word-level tonal ('accent') contrast: high = level pitch across the word, low = pitch fall on the final syllable. Separately, stress (cued by vowel lengthening) has no predictable position according to the authors; one stress minimal pair (initial vs final on a disyllable) is reported, and the authors flag the analysis as provisional ('More testing needs to be done').
new_statements.exceptions: Only one stress-contrastive pair found (/ˈkɔlɔ/ 'bamboo' vs /kɔˈlɔ/ 'skin'); tone marked orthographically on only two pairs (só/so, sagobó/sagobo per Grammar Essentials 2002 §2.1.7). The OPD's syllable-pattern examples bold a single (presumably stressed) syllable in varying positions: E.li, EI.yo, BI.bi, e.BI.ga, ge.le.SI, KOU.da, ho.LAI.so, ge.me.DEI.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated citation forms from an SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet; tone contrast explicitly 'at word level'. The 2002 Grammar Essentials (same authors) repeats the tone statement verbatim and omits stress entirely. A 17-page 2007 OPD Supplement by the same authors exists but could not be opened and may revise the stress/tone analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: All three Hays & Hays documents describe the Kalamo(-Hasalibi) dialect of Odoodee (data collected mainly in Kalamo village, Wawoi Falls); the OPD header reads 'Odoodee (Kalamo) OPD'. Glottolog odoo1238 has no dialect subdivisions; alternate names Ododei, Kalamo, Tomu, Nomad.

sources.note: p.4 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': two-way word-level tone contrast (high = level pitch over the word, low = falling pitch on the last syllable; só 'bird' vs so 'dog', í 'tongue' vs i 'storm'); vowel length non-contrastive, conditioned by stress; 'Stress does not seem to be predictable. More testing needs to be done. Stress was found to be contrastive on only one word (/ˈkɔlɔ/ bamboo vs /kɔˈlɔ/ skin).' Syllable-pattern examples bold one syllable each (e.li, ei.yo, bi.bi, e.BI.ga, ge.le.SI, KOU.da, ho.LAI.so, ge.me.DEI) with no consistent position.
